Francie thought that all the books in the world were in that library and she had a plan about reading all the books in the world. She was reading a book a day in alphabetical order and not skipping the dry ones. She remembered that the first author had been Abbott. She had been reading a book a day for a long time now and she was still in the B's. Already she had read about bees and buffaloes, Bermuda vacations and Byzantine architecture. For her enthusiasm, she had to admit that some of the B's had been hard going. But Francie was a reader.

Every summer, Malik decided he would learn to identify every bird that visited his grandmother's yard, working entirely from a battered field guide missing its back cover. He started with the sparrows because they were the plainest and, he reasoned, the easiest to get out of the way. By July he had moved on to warblers, squinting through binoculars at flickers of yellow in the highest branches, filling a notebook with crossed-out guesses. Some mornings the birds refused to show themselves at all, and Malik simply sat on the porch steps and waited, sure that patience was the last skill the guide couldn't teach him.

Rosa had promised herself she would repair every chair in her late uncle's workshop before selling the building, even the three-legged ones warped beyond any obvious use. She learned to steam bend ash by ruining four strips of wood and consulting a library book so old its spine cracked when opened. Neighbors dropped by to ask when the workshop would finally be listed, and Rosa answered vaguely, already sanding down another armrest. He photocopied star charts at the library and taped them to the refrigerator, and some nights we stood in the cold long after our fingers went numb, arguing about which faint cluster was Cassiopeia and which was simply a smudge on the chart. He never explained why it mattered so much, only that we would finish what he'd started, chart by chart, until the refrigerator was bare.

Delphine had never run more than a mile before she signed up for the marathon, a decision she made mostly to prove something to herself rather than to anyone watching. She trained before dawn so no one would see her walking half the route, kept a log of every blister and every mile she managed to finish, and refused every excuse her body offered her to quit. On race day, she crossed the line four hours after the winner, smiling as though she had won something no clock could measure.

He spent his afternoons hunched over a dictionary held together with tape, filling notebook after notebook with tentative English phrases he crossed out and rewrote. o6.body: The people of medieval Europe have traditionally been seen as uninterested in cleanliness and hygiene, but modern research has shown that this is largely a myth. According to historian Eleanor Janega, most medieval towns in Europe had at least one public bathhouse, which often offered both full-immersion baths and—more affordably—steam baths. While such amenities were available mainly to town dwellers, regular bathing in rivers and streams or daily sponge baths at home were common practices throughout medieval Europe.
o6.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion?

opts.A: It asserts that in medieval Europe steam baths were more popular in rural areas than in urban ones.
opts.B: It describes a limitation of earlier historians' studies of medieval European bathing habits.
opts.C: It concedes that not all people in medieval Europe had access to public bathhouses.
opts.D: It explains why Janega decided to study the popularity of public bathhouses in medieval Europe.

6.1.body: Nineteenth-century factory workers have traditionally been seen as having no access to printed reading material, but modern research has shown that this is largely an oversimplification. According to historian Owen Bracewell, most industrial towns had at least one subscription library that circulated inexpensive serialized novels among workers. While such libraries were concentrated mainly in larger mill towns, informal book-sharing among coworkers and readings aloud during breaks were common practices throughout the industrial regions.
6.1.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion?

opts.A: It asserts that subscription libraries were more common in small towns than in large mill towns.
opts.B: It describes a limitation of earlier historians' research methods.
opts.C: It concedes that not all workers had access to subscription libraries.
opts.D: It explains why Bracewell chose to study industrial-era reading habits.

6.2.body: Rural households in the early twentieth century have traditionally been seen as isolated from national news, but modern research has shown that this view is largely mistaken. According to historian Priya Chandran, most rural counties had at least one shared radio set, often housed in a general store or town hall. While such radios were owned mainly by a handful of wealthier merchants, informal gatherings to listen to broadcasts were common practices throughout rural communities.
6.2.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion?

opts.A: It asserts that radio ownership was more common in rural areas than in cities.
opts.B: It describes a limitation of earlier historians' access to primary sources.
opts.C: It concedes that radio ownership itself was concentrated among a small group.
opts.D: It explains why Chandran decided to focus on rural communities.

6.3.body: Enslaved artisans in the antebellum South have traditionally been seen as excluded from any formal recognition of their craft, but modern research complicates that picture. According to historian Marcus Dell, several enslaved potters and blacksmiths had their work purchased and displayed at regional fairs under their own names. While such recognition was granted mainly by a small number of sympathetic fair organizers, the sale and use of their crafted goods was common practice throughout the region.
6.3.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion?

opts.A: It asserts that fair organizers were generally opposed to recognizing enslaved artisans.
opts.B: It describes a methodological limitation in Dell's own research.
opts.C: It concedes that formal recognition came from only a limited group of organizers.
opts.D: It explains why Dell began investigating regional fairs.

6.4.body: Medieval European peasants have traditionally been seen as having no access to spices beyond salt, but modern research complicates that assumption. According to historian Ingrid Solheim, most manor households kept at least a small store of pepper or mustard seed, often purchased at seasonal markets. While such spices were affordable mainly to peasants with a modest surplus income, growing and using local herbs for flavoring was a common practice throughout the peasantry.
6.4.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion?

opts.A: It asserts that pepper was cheaper than local herbs during the medieval period.
opts.B: It describes a gap in the surviving manorial records Solheim consulted.
opts.C: It concedes that imported spices were out of reach for the poorest peasants.
opts.D: It explains why Solheim focused her research on manor households.

6.5.body: Colonial-era sailors have traditionally been seen as entirely illiterate, but modern research has revised that assumption. According to historian Felix Amaro, most merchant ships carried at least one crew member capable of reading navigational charts and basic correspondence. While full literacy was common mainly among officers and a handful of experienced hands, informal instruction in reading simple logbook entries was practiced throughout many crews.
6.5.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion?

opts.A: It asserts that officers resisted teaching sailors to read.
opts.B: It describes a limitation in the surviving ship logs Amaro examined.
opts.C: It concedes that full literacy was concentrated among a smaller group aboard ship.
opts.D: It explains why Amaro chose to study merchant ships specifically.

o7.body: When classical pianist Martha Argerich performs, it appears as if the music is coming to her spontaneously. She's highly skilled technically, but because of how freely she plays and her willingness to take risks, she seems relaxed and natural. Her apparent ease, however, is due to a tremendous amount of preparation. Despite Argerich's experience and virtuosity, she never takes for granted that she knows a piece of music. Instead, she approaches the music as if encountering it for the first time and tries to understand it anew.

She has extraordinary natural flexibility, but her apparent looseness on the beam comes from years of repeating each transition thousands of times until her body no longer has to think about it. Despite her experience, Duarte still rehearses every routine at quarter speed before competitions, treating even familiar sequences as though a single misplaced habit could still creep back in.

opts.A: To provide details about how Duarte selects her competition routines
opts.B: To assert that Duarte's routines look effortless because of how thoroughly she rehearses them

7.2.body: When chess grandmaster Yusuf Karimov plays, his moves seem to arrive instantly, as though he simply senses the right square without calculation. He is naturally quick, but his apparent speed is the product of thousands of hours spent memorizing patterns from historical games. Despite decades of experience, Karimov still studies each opponent's past matches beforehand, refusing to assume that instinct alone will carry him through an unfamiliar position.
7.2.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

opts.A: To provide details about how Karimov chooses which tournaments to enter
opts.B: To assert that Karimov's speed at the board results from extensive preparation

opts.D: To describe the unique way Karimov approaches unfamiliar opponents

She has a natural feel for flavor, but her calm, unhurried pace on stage comes from rehearsing the same sequence of cuts and plating motions dozens of times beforehand. Even after years of demonstrations, Ferreira still times a full practice run the morning of each show, unwilling to trust that familiarity alone will keep her steady under the lights.
7.3.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

opts.A: To provide details about how Ferreira develops new recipes
opts.B: To assert that Ferreira's stage performances appear smooth because of her extensive rehearsal
opts.C: To discuss which ingredients Ferreira prefers to use in her demonstrations
opts.D: To describe the unique plating style Ferreira has developed over her career

He has considerable natural talent, but his apparent ease comes from slow, deliberate practice sessions in which he isolates and repeats the most difficult passages far more often than the easy ones. Even with a piece he has performed dozens of times, Marchetti still runs through it at half tempo before a concert, refusing to assume his fingers will remember it on their own.
7.4.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

opts.A: To provide details about how Marchetti chooses concertos to perform

She has a naturally warm stage presence, but her apparent spontaneity is the result of rehearsing the same talk dozens of times in front of a mirror until each pause feels natural rather than scripted. Even for talks she has given many times before, Mokoena still rewrites and rehearses her opening lines the night before, unwilling to assume that past success guarantees the same effect again.
7.5.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

opts.A: To provide details about how Mokoena decides which topics to speak about
opts.B: To assert that Mokoena's talks appear spontaneous because of how extensively she rehearses them
opts.C: To discuss the audiences Mokoena finds most comfortable speaking to
opts.D: To describe the unique gestures Mokoena uses while on stage

o8.body:
Text 1: An excavation in Chiquihuite Cave in central Mexico has upended the belief that approximately 13,000 years ago, a group known as the Clovis people were the first human inhabitants of North America. More than 200 crude stone tools were found embedded in a layer of earth that is up to 33,150 years old, revealing that humans occupied the cave thousands of years before the Clovis people reached the continent.

Text 2: The objects uncovered in Chiquihuite Cave are intriguing, but it is premature to characterize them as tools. The stone pieces are so roughly shaped that they may have simply fractured from rocks during natural geological activity in the cave. Moreover, their unearthing has thus far not been accompanied by discoveries of other signs of human activity or even traces of human DNA from surfaces.
o8.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?

opts.A: By agreeing that the stone objects are tools, but disputing their proposed age
opts.B: By questioning whether the stone objects are tools at all, given the lack of other evidence of human presence
opts.C: By arguing that the Clovis people must have created the stone objects themselves
opts.D: By suggesting that the cave was never actually occupied by any humans, ancient or otherwise

8.1.body:
Text 1: Newly analyzed sediment cores from a lakebed in the Andes suggest that a farming settlement existed in the region at least 2,000 years earlier than previously believed. Researchers found layers of pollen from domesticated crops in sediment dated to that earlier period, indicating that organized agriculture began there far sooner than the standard timeline holds.

Text 2: The pollen samples from the Andean lakebed are worth further study, but it is too soon to credit them to deliberate cultivation. The plant species identified also grow wild in the region, and the pollen could have been deposited by wind or animal activity rather than by human planting. No accompanying evidence of tools, irrigation channels, or cleared fields has yet been found at the site.
8.1.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?

opts.A: By agreeing that farming began early, but disputing exactly how early
opts.B: By questioning whether the pollen indicates deliberate farming at all, given the absence of supporting evidence
opts.C: By arguing that the crops were introduced by a different, unrelated culture
opts.D: By suggesting that no plants ever grew wild in the region

8.2.body:
Text 1: A set of markings on a cave wall in northern Spain has been interpreted by one research team as an early calendar tracking lunar cycles, based on the number and spacing of the marks. If correct, this would push back the earliest known evidence of systematic timekeeping by thousands of years.

Text 2: The spacing of the marks on the cave wall is suggestive, but treating them as a calendar goes well beyond what the evidence supports. Similar spacing patterns occur in natural rock fractures found elsewhere in the same cave system, and no other markings at the site show any consistent numerical or seasonal pattern.
8.2.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?

opts.A: By agreeing the marks form a calendar, but disputing how far back it dates
opts.B: By questioning whether the marks are intentional records at all, given similar natural patterns nearby
opts.C: By arguing that a different, later culture must have made the marks
opts.D: By suggesting that no cave markings anywhere can ever be reliably dated

8.3.body:
Text 1: Fragments of woven fabric recovered from a bog in northern Europe have been dated to nearly 9,000 years ago, a finding one research team says proves that organized textile production began far earlier than previously thought.

Text 2: The fabric fragments are a remarkable find, but calling them evidence of organized textile production may be premature. The fibers could have been twisted together informally, without the coordinated tools or techniques that organized production implies, and no spindles or looms have been recovered from the site.
8.3.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?

opts.A: By agreeing that production was organized, but disputing the proposed date
opts.B: By questioning whether the fragments reflect organized production at all, given the lack of tool evidence
opts.C: By arguing that the fabric was brought to the bog from a distant region
opts.D: By suggesting that fabric cannot survive for thousands of years under any conditions

8.4.body:
Text 1: Scratches found on a set of ancient animal bones in East Africa have been interpreted by one team as evidence of early butchery using stone tools, pushing back the timeline for tool-assisted meat processing.

Text 2: The scratches on the bones are intriguing, but attributing them to stone-tool butchery overlooks a simpler explanation. Trampling by other animals across sediment containing small rock fragments can produce very similar marks, and no stone tools have actually been recovered near the bones.
8.4.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?

opts.A: By agreeing tools were used, but disputing which species used them
opts.B: By questioning whether the marks indicate tool use at all, given a plausible natural cause
opts.C: By arguing that the bones belonged to a scavenging species rather than a hunted one
opts.D: By suggesting that the bones are too damaged to study further

8.5.body:
Text 1: Charred plant remains found at a rock shelter in Southeast Asia have been dated to a period thousands of years before the region's earliest known hearths, leading one team to argue that controlled fire use began far earlier than believed.

Text 2: The charred remains are notable, but linking them to controlled fire use is not yet warranted. Wildfires are common in the region, and the site shows no accompanying evidence of a constructed hearth, ash management, or repeated use of a single fire location.
8.5.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?

opts.A: By agreeing fire was controlled, but disputing exactly when it began
opts.B: By questioning whether the remains reflect controlled fire use at all, given the absence of hearth evidence
opts.C: By arguing that a different group must have used the rock shelter first
opts.D: By suggesting that plants cannot be charred by natural wildfires

o9.body: Many literary theorists distinguish between fabula, a narrative's content, and syuzhet, a narrative's arrangement and presentation of events. In the film The Godfather Part II, the fabula is the story of the Corleone family, and the syuzhet is the presentation of the story as it alternates between two timelines in 1901 and 1958. But literary theorist Mikhail Bakhtin maintained that fabula and syuzhet are insufficient to completely describe a narrative—he held that systematic categorizations of artistic phenomena discount the subtle way in which meaning is created by interactions between the artist, the work, and the audience.
o9.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

opts.A: Literary theorist Mikhail Bakhtin argued that there are important characteristics of narratives that are not fully encompassed by two concepts that other theorists have used to analyze narratives.
opts.B: Literary theorist Mikhail Bakhtin claimed that meaning is not inherent in a narrative but is created when an audience encounters a narrative, so that narratives are interpreted differently by different people.
opts.C: The storytelling methods used in The Godfather Part II may seem unusually complicated, but they can be easily understood when two concepts from literary theory are utilized.
opts.D: Narratives that are told out of chronological order are more difficult for audiences to understand than are narratives presented chronologically.

9.1.body: Many economists distinguish between supply shocks, sudden disruptions to production, and demand shocks, sudden shifts in what consumers are willing to buy. During the region's recent fuel shortage, the supply shock was the disrupted shipment of oil, and the demand shock was the resulting shift toward alternative energy sources. But economist Renata Kessler maintained that supply and demand shocks are insufficient to completely explain the shortage's effects—she held that standard categorizations of economic disruption discount the subtle way in which public trust in institutions shapes how quickly markets actually recover.
9.1.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

opts.A: Economist Renata Kessler argued that there are important factors shaping market recovery that are not fully captured by two concepts other economists have used to analyze disruptions.
opts.B: Economist Renata Kessler claimed that supply shocks and demand shocks are simply two different names for the same underlying economic phenomenon.
opts.C: The region's fuel shortage was unusually complex, but it can be fully explained using standard supply and demand analysis.
opts.D: Public trust in institutions matters more to a region's economy than supply and demand shocks do.

9.2.body: Many musicologists distinguish between melody, a piece's sequence of pitches, and harmony, the combination of pitches sounded together. In a given jazz standard, the melody is the tune a listener might hum, and the harmony is the underlying chords supporting it. But musicologist Deshawn Fields maintained that melody and harmony are insufficient to completely describe a performance—he held that standard categorizations of musical structure discount the subtle way in which a performer's timing and phrasing shape a listener's emotional experience.
9.2.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

opts.A: Musicologist Deshawn Fields argued that there are important aspects of a musical performance that are not fully captured by two concepts other musicologists have used to analyze music.
opts.B: Musicologist Deshawn Fields claimed that melody and harmony are ultimately the same musical element viewed from two different perspectives.
opts.C: Jazz standards are unusually difficult to analyze, but melody and harmony are sufficient tools for understanding them.
opts.D: A performer's timing and phrasing matter more to a jazz standard than its melody and harmony do.

9.3.body: Many linguists distinguish between denotation, a word's literal dictionary meaning, and connotation, the associations a word carries beyond that meaning. In a given poem, the denotation of a word might be its plain definition, and the connotation might be the mood that word evokes. But linguist Anya Petrenko maintained that denotation and connotation are insufficient to completely describe a word's effect in a poem—she held that standard categorizations of meaning discount the subtle way in which a word's placement and rhythm within a line shape how a reader experiences it.
9.3.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

opts.A: Linguist Anya Petrenko argued that there are important aspects of a word's poetic effect that are not fully captured by two concepts other linguists have used to analyze meaning.
opts.B: Linguist Anya Petrenko claimed that denotation and connotation are simply two labels for a single, unified concept of meaning.
opts.C: Poems are unusually difficult texts, but denotation and connotation are sufficient tools for analyzing them.
opts.D: A word's placement and rhythm within a line matter more than its denotation and connotation do.

9.4.body: Many architects distinguish between form, a building's physical shape, and function, the practical purposes the building serves. In a given train station, the form is its arched glass roof, and the function is its role in moving passengers efficiently. But architectural critic Soren Vik maintained that form and function are insufficient to completely describe a building's significance—he held that standard categorizations of design discount the subtle way in which a building's relationship to its surrounding neighborhood shapes how residents come to feel about it.
9.4.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

opts.A: Architectural critic Soren Vik argued that there are important aspects of a building's significance that are not fully captured by two concepts other critics have used to analyze design.
opts.B: Architectural critic Soren Vik claimed that form and function are ultimately identical concepts described using different vocabulary.
opts.C: Train stations are unusually complex buildings, but form and function are sufficient tools for analyzing them.
opts.D: A building's relationship to its neighborhood matters more than its form and function do.

9.5.body: Many anthropologists distinguish between kinship by blood, ties based on biological descent, and kinship by practice, ties formed through shared daily life and obligation. In a given community, kinship by blood might describe siblings, and kinship by practice might describe long-term neighbors who share caregiving duties. But anthropologist Idris Okonjo maintained that these two categories are insufficient to completely describe how community bonds actually form—he held that standard categorizations of kinship discount the subtle way in which shared hardship over time can create obligations as strong as either category alone.
9.5.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

opts.A: Anthropologist Idris Okonjo argued that there are important aspects of community bonds that are not fully captured by two concepts other anthropologists have used to analyze kinship.
opts.B: Anthropologist Idris Okonjo claimed that kinship by blood and kinship by practice describe exactly the same relationships in every community.
opts.C: Community bonds are unusually difficult to study, but kinship by blood and kinship by practice are sufficient tools for understanding them.
opts.D: Shared hardship matters more to a community than either kinship by blood or kinship by practice does.

o13.body: As media consumption has become increasingly multiplatform and socially mediated, active news acquisition has diminished in favor of an attitude known as "news finds me" (NFM), in which people passively rely on their social networks and ambient media environments for information about current events.
